'''''Staurastrum''''' is a large [[genus (biology)|genus]] of desmids ([[Desmidiaceae]]),<ref>See the [[National Center for Biotechnology Information|NCBI]] [https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/Taxonomy/Browser/wwwtax.cgi?mode=Info&id=31317 webpage on Staurastrum].  Data extracted from the {{cite web | url=https://ftp.ncbi.nih.gov/pub/taxonomy/ | title=NCBI taxonomy resources | publisher=[[National Center for Biotechnology Information]] | access-date=2007-03-19}}</ref> a group of [[green algae]] closely related to the land plants ([[Embryophyta]]).<ref name="pmid12569426">{{cite journal |vauthors=Gontcharov AA, Marin BA, Melkonian MA |title=Molecular phylogeny of conjugating green algae (Zygnemophyceae, Streptophyta) inferred from SSU rDNA sequence comparisons |journal=J. Mol. Evol. |volume=56 |issue=1 |pages=89–104 |date=January 2003 |pmid=12569426 |doi=10.1007/s00239-002-2383-4}}</ref><ref>See the [[National Center for Biotechnology Information|NCBI]] [https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/Taxonomy/Browser/wwwtax.cgi?mode=Info&id=33100 webpage on Cosmarium].  Data extracted from the {{cite web | url=https://ftp.ncbi.nih.gov/pub/taxonomy/ | title=NCBI taxonomy resources | publisher=[[National Center for Biotechnology Information]] | access-date=2007-03-19}}</ref> Members of this genus are microscopic and found in [[freshwater]] habitats around the world.

The name ''Staurastrum'' comes from the Greek roots ''stauron'', meaning "cross", and ''astron'', meaning "star".<ref name=CarolinaLucidKey>{{cite web|url=https://fmp.conncoll.edu/Silicasecchidisk/LucidKeys3.5/Keys_v3.5/Carolina35_Key/Media/Html/Staurastrum_Main.html|title=Staurastrum|first1= Hannah|last1= Shayler|first2=Peter A.|last2=Siver|work=Carolina Lucid Key to Freshwater Algae|publisher=Connecticut College | date=2004 |access-date=2024-11-28 }}</ref>

==Description==
''Staurastrum'' consists of singular cells with two identical halves, called semicells; in most species, the cell is deeply constricted at the middle, making the division between semicells clear. When viewed from the polar axis, they are biradiate (with two planes of symmetry) or pluriradiate (with more than two planes of symmetry).<ref name=Hall2014>{{cite book |editor-first1=John D.|editor-last1=Wehr|editor-first2=Robert G.|editor-last2=Sheath|editor-first3=J. Patrick|editor-last3=Kociolek |date= 2014 |edition=2 |title= Freshwater Algae of North America: Ecology and Classification |last1= Hall|first1=John D.| last2=McCourt |first2=Richard M. |chapter= Chapter 9. Conjugating Green Algae Including Desmids |url= |location= |publisher= Elsevier Inc. |page= |isbn=978-0-12-385876-4 }}</ref> Biradiate individuals have long, arm-shaped extensions (termed "processes") attached to the main body of the semicells. Pluriradiate individuals may lack these processes. The [[cell wall]] is either smooth, or covered with granules or spines. In each semicell there is a [[chloroplast]], usually located axially, with radiating lobes and/or ridges; some species have parietally located chloroplasts.<ref name=EuropeanFlora>{{cite book|title= European flora of the desmid genera ''Staurastrum'' and ''Staurodesmus''|last1= Coesel|first1= P.F.M.|last2= Meesters|first2=J.|date=2013|pages= 357|publisher= KNNV Publishing|location= Zeist|isbn= 978-90-04-27791-5}}</ref>

===Identification===
''Staurastrum'' as a genus is usually easy to identify, due to its long processes and symmetry. Some smaller species, particularly those without long processes, can be confused with ''[[Cosmarium]]'', but that genus has biradiate (not pluriradiate) cells and never with long processes. The smaller species may also be confused with ''[[Tetraedron]]'' or various [[xanthophyte]] algae, but differ in shape, ornamentation, and chloroplast morphology.<ref name=Hall2014/>

Although some species of ''Staurastrum'' are unmistakable, identification of species within the genus is often difficult. Important characters for identification include the degree of radiation (the number of planes of symmetry), overall shape and size of the cells, and the distribution and type of ornamentation on the cell wall. As with other genera of desmids, identification is complicated by the fact that these algae exhibit considerable phenotypic variability.<ref name=EuropeanFlora/>

==Taxonomy==
''Staurastrum'' is the second largest genus of desmids (after ''Cosmarium''), with about 800 species. It is the most heterogeneous desmid genus, and has been described as a [[wastebin taxon]].<ref name=Teiling>{{cite journal | title=The genus ''Staurodesmus'': A taxonomic study | last1=Teiling | first1=Einar | journal=Arkiv för Botanik | volume=6 | issue=11 | pages=467–629 }}</ref> Several attempts have been made to dismantle the genus and split it up into smaller, more homogeneous units, such as [[G. M. Palamar-Mordvintseva]]'s segregate genera ''Cylindriastrum'', ''Cosmoastrum'', and ''Raphidiastrum''. These attempts have not been widely accepted, because they are also arbitrary.<ref>{{cite book|title= Desmids of the Lowlands. 2nd revised & extended edition|last1= Coesel|first1=P.F.M.|last2= Meesters|first2= K.[J.]|location= Zeist|publisher= KNNV Uitgeverij|pages= 424|isbn= 9789050119481}}</ref>

''Staurastrum'' is not [[monophyletic]], as molecular phylogenetic studies have shown that members of the genus are dispersed across many clades; however, a "core" ''Staurastrum'' clade was resolved.<ref>{{cite journal|doi=10.1111/j.0022-3646.2005.04165.x |title=Molecular Phylogeny of ''Staurastrum'' Meyen ex Ralfs and Related Genera (Zygnematophyceae, Streptophyta) Based On Coding And Noncoding rDNA Sequence Comparisons |date=2005 |last1=Gontcharov |first1=Andrey A. |last2=Melkonian |first2=Michael |journal=Journal of Phycology |volume=41 |issue=4 |pages=887–899 }}</ref> The genus is still in use, because there is no known way of classifying desmids in line with their evolutionary history.<ref name=EuropeanFlora/>

==Habitat and distribution==
''Staurastrum'', as well as other desmid genera, live primarily in acidic lakes, ponds, and swamps with low nutrient levels. They usually live on [[sediment]]s or [[Periphyton|submerged surfaces]]. A number of species are characteristic of [[eutrophic]] waters and are [[planktonic]].<ref>{{cite journal | doi= 10.1127/algol_stud/80/1996/9 | title= Three new planktic Staurastrum taxa (Chlorophyta, Desmidiaceae) from eutrophic water bodies and the significance of microspecies in desmid taxonomy | date= 1996 | last1= Coesel | first1= Peter F. M. | last2= Joosten | first2= Anton M. T. | journal= Algological Studies/Archiv für Hydrobiologie, Supplement Volumes | volume= 80 | pages= 9–20 }}</ref>

Many species have a [[cosmopolitan distribution]].<ref>{{cite book| last1=Wehr |first1=John D. |last2=Sheath |first2=Robert G. |title=Freshwater Algae of North America |contributor-last=Gerrath |contributor-first=Joseph F. |contribution=Conjugating Green Algae and Desmids |publisher=Elsevier Inc. |date=2003}}</ref> However, some species are restricted to a particular [[biogeographic realm]].<ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.1007/BF00010818 |title=5. Biogeography of desmids |year=1996 |last1=Coesel |first1=Peter F. M. |journal=Hydrobiologia |volume=336 |issue=1–3 |pages=41–53 |s2cid=11752270 |url=https://dare.uva.nl/personal/pure/en/publications/biography-of-desmids(399d4eaf-b8c0-47b6-85f2-45d74b4e151d).html }}</ref>
